support.locus: RV 7.81.3a, 7.81.5c, 8.47.14b, 10.70.6a (38 RV padas with div- + duhitár-)

cognate: Ved. diváḥ (gen. of dyú-/div-) = Gk Διός < *diwós; Ved. duhitár- = Gk θυγάτηρ < *dʰugh₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: referent drift: in the RV the 'daughter of heaven' is Uṣas (Dawn); in Homer the same title goes to Aphrodite, Athena, Ate, Persephone, Artemis. Word order is free in both (diváḥ duhitā́ / duhitar divaḥ; Διὸς θυγάτηρ / θυγάτηρ Διός).
shared_syntax: genitive of the sky-god + kinship noun 'daughter', used as an appositive title of a goddess (nominative or vocative)
context: RV 1.92.5d: Dawn, 'daughter of heaven', has set up her bright beam; Il. 3.374 the title-holder is Aphrodite, rescuer of Paris, Il. 4.515 Athena rousing the Achaeans: in both traditions it is the fixed honorific of a female deity, not a description made on the spot

cognate: Ved. dyaùḥ/dyaúḥ = Gk Ζεῦ(ς) < *dyēws; Ved. pítar/pitā́ = Gk πάτερ < *ph₂tér/*ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: none in wording; in Vedic Dyaus is a receding figure paired with Earth-mother (merism dyaúḥ pitā́ pṛthivī́ mātā́), in Greek Zeus is the head of the pantheon. Latin fused the vocative into Iūpiter (recalled).
shared_syntax: divine name + 'father' as an address formula; RV 6.51.5a is a true vocative with the second word unaccented (dyaùḥ pítar), exactly like Ζεῦ πάτερ, an invocation at the start of a prayer
context: RV 6.51.5a invokes 'Father Sky, Mother Earth' for mercy; Il. 19.121 Hera opens her address to Zeus with Ζεῦ πάτερ: both are prayer-openings

cognate: Latv. Dieva (gen. of Dievs < *deywós) and Gk Διός- (< *diwós, gen. of *dyēws) come from one root; Ved. diváḥ is the same genitive as the Greek
drift_or_renewal: the 'son' word is renewed in each branch: Latv. dēls, Gk κοῦρος, Ved. nápāt- (dual nápātā); Latvian has the derived *deywós 'god' where Greek and Vedic keep the genitive of *dyēws
shared_syntax: genitive of the sky-god + 'son(s)' as the name or title of divine youths
context: BV 4989: the singer climbs a pea-stalk to heaven and sees 'God's son saddling his horse'. The Greek Διόσκουροι are horsemen (HH 33.18 ταχέων ἐπιβήτορες ἵππων) and the Vedic 'sons of heaven' are the Aśvins, the 'horsemen' twins. All three are divine young men tied to horses: the Indo-European divine twins (recalled).
phrase: 'son(s) of *dyeu-' (son-word renewed in each branch): the horse-riding sons of the sky god

cognate: Ved. sū́rya- = Gk ἥλιος/ἠέλιος < *sóh₂wl̥; Ved. spáś- 'watcher, spy' and Gk σκοπός 'watcher' (from *speḱ- with the metathesis σκεπ-/σκοπ-) share one root
drift_or_renewal: Greek has the o-grade agent noun σκοπός (σκοπ- by the usual metathesis) where Vedic has the root noun spáś-; the Greek genitive merism 'of gods and men' matches Vedic 'of all that moves' (RV 4.13.3) with different words
shared_syntax: the Sun called 'watcher' (agent noun from *speḱ-) with a genitive of whom he watches: spáśam víśvasya jágataḥ (RV 4.13.3) ~ θεῶν σκοπὸν ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν (HH Dem. 62); RV 1.33.8d puts the watchers (spáśaḥ) beside the sun
context: HH Dem. 62: Demeter and Hecate go to Helios, 'watcher of gods and men', because he sees everything; RV 4.13.3: the mares carry the Sun, 'the watcher of the whole moving world'; RV 1.33.8d/7.87.3a: the gods' watchers set all round. In both the all-seeing sun is a spy or witness

cognate: Ved. amŕ̥ta- = Gk ἄμβροτος < *n̥-mr̥-tó- 'undying'; Ved. a-jára- and Gk ἀ-γήρως both privatives of *ǵerh₂- 'grow old'
drift_or_renewal: Homer renews the 'undying' half of the doublet with ἀθάνατος (ἀθάνατος καὶ ἀγήρως, 9×) and keeps the cognate ἄμβροτος as an epithet of a god (θεὸς ἄμβροτος, the anchor); the 'ageless' half is cognate in both
shared_syntax: two privative adjectives, 'ageless' + 'undying', predicated of a divine being; in the anchors amŕ̥tā and ἄμβροτος each qualify a deity (Uṣas; Hermes)
context: RV 1.113.13d: Dawn, 'unageing, immortal', moves by her own power; Il. 24.460: Hermes tells Priam, whom he calls γέρον 'old man', that he is θεὸς ἄμβροτος. In both the god is set against ageing mortals; Homer's ageless-and-immortal formula is the stock description of divine status (Od. 5.136, 5.218).

cognate: Ved. dhr̥ṣ- (dhr̥ṣánt-, dhr̥ṣṇú-) = Gk θαρσ-/θρασ- < *dʰers-; Ved. mánas- = Gk μένος < *ménos
drift_or_renewal: drift: mánas- 'mind' vs μένος 'fighting spirit, might'. Renewal: the anchor Il. 16.242 and the slab's Hesiod/Bacchylides lines have ἦτορ where the Homeric support has μένος, and RV 1.54.4b has tmán- 'self' with the same participle; ātmán/tmán- and ἦτορ are probably not cognate
shared_syntax: adjective or verb from *dʰers- qualifying the inner force of a hero or god: dhr̥ṣát mánaḥ 'bold mind', compound dhr̥ṣán-manas-; Gk μένος πολυθαρσές 'very bold might', μένος καὶ θάρσος, θαρσύνω ἦτορ 'to embolden the heart'
context: RV 1.54.3-4: Indra, 'whose mind is bold', who 'with bold self' split Śambara: a warrior god's courage. Il. 16.242: Achilles prays Zeus to embolden Patroclus' heart for battle; the μένος πολυθαρσές lines are a god putting fighting courage into a hero. Both are courage for combat located in an inner faculty.

cognate: Ved. vŕ̥ka- = ORu вълкъ < *wĺ̥kʷos; Ved. pánthā-/path- = ORu путь < *pónth₂-/*pn̥th₂-
drift_or_renewal: the verbs differ (Ved. sedh- 'keep away', with tárantam 'crossing' the waters; ORu прѣ-рыскати 'run across'); in the ORu the wolf is a man in wolf form (Vseslav)
shared_syntax: a wolf in relation to a path in the sky: Ved. patháḥ vŕ̥kam (abl. path + acc. wolf, the wolf kept from the paths as it crosses) ~ ORu влъкомъ путь прерыскаше (instr. 'as a wolf' + acc. path + 'ran across')
context: RV 1.105.11: eagles sitting 'in the middle of the ascent of heaven' keep the wolf, as he crosses the waters, off the paths; 1.105.18 the ruddy wolf saw the poet on the path. Slovo o polku Igoreve 159: Vseslav, running as a wolf by night, 'crossed the path of great Khors', the sun god. In both a wolf crosses a celestial path, a light-god's road. Cf. the Norse wolf that follows the sun (Grímnismál 40).

cognate: Ved. rájas- = Gk ἔρεβος (ἐρεβεννός) < *h₁régʷos 'darkness'; Ved. nákt- = Gk νύξ < *nókʷts
drift_or_renewal: drift: Ved. rájas- has moved from 'darkness' to 'airspace, region' and needs kr̥ṣṇá- 'black' to be dark again; Greek keeps 'darkness' (Ἔρεβος, ἐρεβεννός). The colour adjective is renewed (kr̥ṣṇá- ~ μέλαινα)
shared_syntax: *h₁régʷos-material with 'night' or 'black': náktam ... rájobhiḥ, kr̥ṣṇā́ rájāṃsi ~ ἐρεβεννὴ νύξ, Ἔρεβος ... μέλαινα Νύξ
context: RV 1.116.20 the Aśvins carry their protégé 'by night through the spaces'; RV 1.35.2/4 Savitar travels through the black space, i.e. the night sky; Homer's ἐρεβεννὴ νύξ falls or covers the dying; Hesiod's Erebos and black Night are sibling children of Chaos. In both the word for 'darkness' is attached to night

note: All 195 bundles read. Most bundles pair Vedic with Greek prose (Aristotle, Hippocrates, orators) and hold nothing. Claims: 2 high (divo duhitā/Διὸς θυγάτηρ; dyaùṣ pitar/Ζεῦ πάτερ), 4 medium, 2 low. Leads tested and dropped: pṛṣṭá- ... pṛthivyā́m ~ OE on foldan gefrægen (Beo. 1197), nā́bhā pṛthivyā́ḥ (slab Greek has only a body navel), ūrdhvá- sthā- ~ ὀρθὸς ἵστημι, bhid- śíras ~ cerebrum finditur, rakṣ- ~ ἀλέξω, stan- abhrá ~ στένω νέφος. All were generic or out of context. The Latvian daina corpus lives under raw/books and is off limits, so it was not searched.
